To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the construction and management processes of the funding formulae in each LEA were incremental in nature, and that the funding formulae produced were predominantly incrementalist in effect.
the construction of the new funding formulae was incrementalist, and that this was a consequence of the way the teams were constituted and their relationship with the central LEA administration.

, in the three LEAs we studied, the funding formulae were constructed in a way that preserved historical expenditure patterns, and that this was achieved through a combination of factors, including the lack of information on school costs, the lack of a clear definition of the budgeting parameters, the lack of an agreed set of cost elements and the use of incrementalism as a strategy to preserve the status quo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the funding formulae for LMS were constructed and managed.
the processes through which the funding formulae were constructed.
the construction of a new funding formula in the context of the introduction of LMS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

incrementalism in education budgeting is not the result of an ideological preference for incrementalism but rather of the constraints that operate on incrementalism in education and which are, to some extent, peculiar to the education system.
the funding formulae in the three LEAs were incremental in nature.

the funding formulae in each case were incrementalist and that, as such, they reflected the interests of those groups who benefited from the status quo, and who had the most to lose if the budgeting system became comprehensive and more radical.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the funding formulae were constructed incrementally and, in this sense, were not comprehensive.

the funding formulae produced by each LMS team were a product of a process of negotiation between the central and the school‐based managers, and that, as a result, the funding formulae reflected a compromise between the central and school managers’ perceptions of what was a fair and appropriate budget.
the LMS funding formulae were not only based on incremental budgeting but also on incrementalism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the funding formulae were not the product of a rational process of decision making but rather the outcome of a complex process of negotiation between different stakeholders.
, despite the 1988 Act's emphasis on comprehensiveness, the funding formulas developed by the LMS teams in our case studies were predominantly incremental in nature.
the LMS teams in each of the three LEAs we studied were not able to produce a comprehensive funding formula.
